newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: India, Pakistan put Kashmir on peace talks agenda.
newsitem.headline: India, Pakistan put Kashmir on peace talks agenda.

text.p: India and Pakistan, seeking to put 50 years of hostility behind them, on Monday announced an agenda for peace talks that includes the Kashmir dispute.

A joint statement issued after weekend talks between the Indian and Pakistani foreign ministry secretaries, or top career diplomats, said the two sides had agreed to set up working groups to tackle all outstanding issues dividing them.
India and Pakistan, both seen as threshold nuclear powers, agreed to halt hostile propaganda and avoid provocative actions.
Topping the agenda was "peace and security, including CBMs (confidence-building measures)", with Jammu and Kashmir second.
The two countries have fought two of their three wars since independence from Britain in 1947 over Kashmir, two thirds of which is controlled by India and the rest by Pakistan.
India and Pakistan agreed to discuss their confrontation on the Siachen Glacier, terrorism and drug trafficking, economic and commercial cooperation, and other issues.

The statement followed talks that started on Friday between delegations led by foreign ministry secretaries Shamshad Ahmad of Pakistan and Salman Haider of India, which it said had been held in a "cordial and constructive atmosphere".
It said the foreign secretaries would hold a third round of talks in September in New Delhi. The first ice-breaking session took place in the Indian capital in late March.
Asked when the two prime ministers might meet again, Pakistani Foreign Ministry spokesman Khalid Saleem said this would happen "when the time is ripe", but gave no date.

Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral and his Pakistani opposite number Nawaz Sharif met in the Maldives last month at a regional summit. Last week they had their first chat on a telephone hotline newly installed between their two offices.
In a separate statement, the two sides said they had agreed to release Indian and Pakistani fishermen and boats detained for straying into each other's territorial waters.
They agreed to free 26 Pakistani boats and 195 crew and 35 Indian boats and 194 crew. "Other boats and crew will be released as and when identified," the joint statement said.
"I am happy to state that we have successfully completed the first stage of the task entrusted to us by our two prime ministers," Ahmad told a joint news conference.
"The two sides have agreed to address all outstanding issues with a view to achieving the goal of good neighbourly and cooperative relations," he said in a prepared statement.
"We hope the mechanism on which we have agreed will initiate progress towards the settlement of all outstanding issues listed in the joint statement.
"On our part, we will continue the dialogue with sincerity and serious purpose. We have no illusions about the complexity of the work ahead of us.
"It is important for both sides now to take steps to create conditions conducive to make the process purposeful and result-oriented," Ahmad added.
Haider said in reply that he believed the agreement "provides the basis for comprehensive, constructive and sustained dialogue between India and Pakistan".
"It is our purpose that the dialogue leads to establishment of trust, friendship and cooperation between the two countries," Haider said.

Saleem brushed aside questions on whether the negotiators had discussed the reported movement of Indian Prithvi missiles towards the Pakistani border or firing incidents across the Line of Control that divides Kashmir. New Delhi has denied that the medium-range Prithvi missiles have been deployed.
"We have diplomatic relations, we are constantly talking to each other," Saleem said when pressed on the missile issue. "So this is not the only forum on which we talk to each other."
Haider said no deadline had been set for setting up the working groups, on which the modalities have yet to be agreed.
Quoting an Urdu couplet, his Pakistani counterpart said: "Veils on doors will be lifted slowly, slowly."
